title: European Club Cup: Amateurs rub shoulders with the pros
summary:
While looking through the standings of the European Club Cup which concluded last week, René Mandelbaum focused on the teams at the bottom of the table. To his surprise, he discovered that many of their players were rated between 1800 and 2000. These are good club players - still, he had expected stronger opposition at a European championship. "With a field like this, we shouldn't finish last", he thought. | Photos: SK Weisse Dame Hamburg

Looking back at the European Club Cup

By René Mandelbaum

The months flew by, but the idea remained. Some research revealed that each country may nominate five teams for the tournament if that country runs a league competition.

That might explain the relatively weak teams from smaller countries, but not the relatively weak teams from Germany.

Unlike in football or handball, in chess it is possible to play for clubs in different countries at the same time. Cristiano Ronaldo cannot play one weekend in the Spanish league, the next in the Swedish league and then in the German league. In chess, however, this is an important source of income for second-tier professionals. The financial backers of German Bundesliga clubs apparently have less interest in paying their professionals to play in the European Club Cup. That could explain why the German teams tend to field amateur players. At least, that is how this correspondent pieced things together.

An enquiry with the sporting director then revealed that Bundesliga clubs have to confirm by the beginning of August whether they want to take part. If they do not, other clubs can apply.

That is how SK Weisse Dame Hamburg, a team from the Landesliga, the fourth tier, came to receive a place in the event.

Things then had to move very quickly, as there was only one week left until the registration deadline.

Would the first-team players be able to get time off work? Who had the time, the inclination and the money? Would it fit around university? Could two days off school be arranged? For students? For teachers?

These hurdles could be overcome. Not all of the first-team players were available, but seven motivated players were quickly found (the matches are played over six boards, so taking a reserve player seemed sensible).

The entry fee was transferred and flights were booked. Since the event had been advertised with the very attractive Medun hotel complex in Herceg Novi (Montenegro), three of our players also decided to bring their wives/girlfriends (and children).

Two weeks before the tournament began, one of our players wrote in the WhatsApp group that he had read on the tournament website that the venue had changed.

We only received official information about this a few days before travelling. That was somewhat surprising. Suddenly the venue was in Budva. It is only 45 km from the original venue, but the drive was said to take 1 hour and 15 minutes, including a ferry crossing.

"Nothing we can do about it - somehow everything will work out". The reviews of the new hotel complex were not particularly good, however, if the relevant online review sites were to be believed.

"Bite the bullet"

On Friday, 23 October, half of our team landed in Dubrovnik at around 4 p.m., one of the recommended airports. Dubrovnik is in neighbouring Croatia.

Players from all over the world were arriving at the airport and were then directed onto a coach. Even though there must already have been 50 people on board, it did not leave.

Another flight had been delayed, so we waited for 90 minutes. Then the journey finally began. At least for 15 minutes. We then reached the border with Montenegro. Unlike Croatia, Montenegro is not part of the Schengen Area. We stood there waiting for a good two hours, closer to three. Then everyone on the coach had to get out, present their passport individually to the border officer and cross the border on foot.

Eventually we were able to get back on the coach and continue. At around 11 p.m. we reached the hotel complex. Those had been seven rather unpleasant hours.

Fortunately, the other half of the team had flown via Podgorica Airport. That is already in Montenegro, which avoids the congestion at the border. The opening ceremony, however, was described by the other half of the team as very disappointing. Very few participants attended and there was little atmosphere. There was a speech in the local language with English subtitles and a short performance by a musical group.

The next disappointment was the rooms. We had originally booked suites in a four-star hotel for no less than €99 per person in a double room. Had our accommodation been booked through an online portal, it would have cost only half as much.

There was no hot water and the condition of the rooms was dreadful. They were draughty, cold and not very clean.

The hotel complex has several different blocks, as we discovered during a late-night exchange with chess friends from other clubs. We had ended up in the worst one. Complaining at reception achieved nothing: "Contact the organiser".

So we slept in our jackets and without showering. The following morning we were moved to other blocks. The rooms were clean and the water was hot. But we had imagined a suite in a four-star hotel to be somewhat differently.

The family room promised to one of our players, however, did not exist. Nor did a baby's crib. He then moved to a completely different hotel. Whether he will ever get his money back from the organiser is unknown.

The food, however, was acceptable. Suddenly finding yourself in the buffet queue behind a chess legend such as Vishy Ivanchuk partially made up for the trouble.

The weather was also pleasantly warm during the day, and we were able to swim in the sea.

The playing hall was a large tent in which all the games were played. This meant you could look directly over the shoulders of the superstars. "Giri looked at my board for half a minute. He probably hasn't seen a position with two queens against three very often", one of our players said of his personal highlight.

You were not allowed to take your own photos in the playing hall, however. Mobile phones had to be left outside and there were strict checks at the entrance.

Only during the evening blitz tournaments was there an opportunity to take your own pictures in the playing hall. Otherwise, you had to rely on the tournament photographers, of whom there were fortunately always plenty around, and they also took pictures at the lower boards.

The rounds always began at 2 p.m. Those who wished could therefore spend the morning exploring Budva's attractive old town or taking short excursions.

In the evenings, many players sat around the pool area, where the bar stayed open until 11 p.m. Drinks of all kinds were included. One of our players, Ben Erk, managed to get a photo with well-known streamers and Matthias Bluebaum (see title image).

From a chess perspective, the tournament was tough for us. We did, however, manage to achieve our goal of winning at least two matches and finishing ahead of nine teams.

The professional teams finished at the top, mostly assembled squads whose players are rather unlikely to be found attending their club's regular blitz night.

Behind them came strong amateur teams keen to play against strong opposition, but also teams of retirees for whom the event was simply an enjoyable group trip - in other words, a colourful cross-section of the European chess scene.

At the prize-giving ceremony, which has already been covered in the two articles below, we noticed that those receiving the awards hardly seemed to celebrate at all. Had we been invited onto the stage, we would have cheered quite differently. The chess world really missed out there. Unfortunately, however, only the top three were honoured.

Despite a few difficulties, taking part in the European Club Cup was a great experience for us.

title: KCF Academy: Third Season Highlights
summary:
The Kasparov Chess Foundation Academy has wrapped up its third season, marking another important year of growth for the organization, with expanding educational programs, international events, and outstanding achievements by participants in KCF programs. And the momentum isn't slowing down: registration is now open for the KCF Academy 2027 season, a six-month online training program for ambitious chess players around the world.

Third Season Highlights and a New Chapter for 2027

This year, KCFA helped organize the Kasparov Chess Festival in Radenci, which brought together 650 chess players from 33 countries. Following the tournament, the Academy held its international chess camp, welcoming 65 young players from around the world for chess training, swimming, and other activities. One of the highlights was a visit to the Kasparov Grand Tour, where participants had the opportunity to meet Garry Kasparov for a special photo and autograph session.

The season also featured the highly successful Garry Kasparov Trainers Conference, attended by 150 participants.

KCF Academy is especially proud of its educational program, which is built on Botvinnik’s four-level system. Just as important are our other formats, such as the Practical Workshops and the Star Lessons, where students have the joy of learning from legendary players like Kasparov, Topalov, Aronian, Svidler, Caruana and others.

In 2026, the Academy launched a special program for national Olympic teams, offered on preferential terms. We work closely with KCF trainers, who coach a selected group of the most talented juniors from around the world. The highlight of KCF training is the annual live camp led by Garry Kasparov during the Zagreb Grand Tour, where he works with this select group of top young talents. For the next generation, we held a special selection camp in Munich with Roman Vidonyak, one of the world’s leading trainers, supported by Chess Club Bayern.

Participants in Kasparov Chess Foundation programs achieved remarkable results this season: Anastasia Hnatyshyn of Ukraine became European Women's Champion, with congratulations to her coaches Volodymyr Grabinsky and Adrian Mikhalchishin. Other outstanding achievements included Ihor Samunenkov, who became European Team Champion with Ukraine in 2025, and Lukas Dotzer, a European Youth medalist. At the 2026 European Youth Rapid Championship, Bozhena Piddubna and Maksym Pankiv, both from Ukraine, became champions, while Maksym Dubnevych and Peter Balint earned medals.

IGM Ihor Samunenkov won the gold medal at the 2026 Samarkand Olympiad, finishing ahead of World Champion Gukesh. Samarkand was also the setting for a historic milestone: at just 11 years old, Bodhana Sivanandan secured her final WGM norm, becoming the youngest Woman Grandmaster in history.

The third season reflects the Academy's growing international community and its commitment to developing the next generation of chess players, coaches, and champions.

Registration Opens for KCF Academy 2027

Building on this success, the Academy now turns to its next season. From January 9 to June 23, 2027, participants will follow a structured program combining level-based training, thematic workshops, and exclusive masterclasses with some of the greatest names in chess.

A major highlight of the new season will be six exclusive masterclasses with Veselin Topalov , former World Champion and former world number one. Known for his dynamic and uncompromising style, Topalov will share insights from his exceptional career, focusing on attacking play, preparation, critical decision-making, and performing under pressure.

The KCF STARS Masterclass Series will also feature a special masterclass with Garry Kasparov , the 13th World Champion and founder of the Kasparov Chess Foundation, alongside lectures by other elite grandmasters and internationally renowned coaches.

KCF Academy conducts a 6 hour training package for different levels in a week. This year it will be as usual 4 levels plus Expert level for National teams and strong club players.

Beyond the online curriculum, all KCF Academy members will also be able to take part in the Kasparov Chess Foundation Friendship Festival 2027. The festival brings together players from around the world for top-level tournaments, training, friendship and unique chess experiences. It gives Academy members a special opportunity to meet in person, compete internationally and become part of the wider KCF community. Members can also look forward to more camps with top trainers, following the very successful one already held.

Preseason Special

Ahead of the main 2027 season, KCF Academy is also offering a Preseason Special program, giving players an early opportunity to train with the Academy before the full curriculum begins.

The program includes:

10 live lectures, each 90 minutes long

Every Saturday at 18:00 CET

Program dates: October 17 – December 19, 2027

Live on Zoom – participate from anywhere

All materials are available on the KCF Academy App, which means every participant can watch any lesson, Master Class or Star Lesson at any time.

Focus on strategic and practical thinking in chess

The Main Season runs from January 9 to June 23, 2027, offering a complete online chess training experience led by Garry Kasparov and a team of world- class grandmasters. For more information and to join, visit https://www.kcfacademy.org
